title: Food & drink
goal: Order food and drinks, say you're hungry or thirsty, say what you like and don't like, and accept or refuse more.
intro:
In Nepal, **खाना** 'food/meal' usually means **दाल भात तरकारी** — rice, lentil soup and vegetable curry — eaten twice a day. Snacks in between are **खाजा**: momos, noodles, beaten rice, tea.

The key grammar here is the **experiencer construction** with **लाई**: Nepali doesn't say 'I am hungry' or 'I like momos' but 'hunger has struck *to me*' (मलाई भोक लाग्यो) and 'momos fall into the heart *to me*' (मलाई मःम मन पर्छ).

vocab.note: खाना खानु 'to eat a meal'. Without context often means dal bhat.
Also stands for 'a proper meal'. Raw rice is चामल chāmal.
Freshly made tomato/sesame achar is served with momos and dal bhat.
बफ baph 'buffalo meat' (from English 'buff') is the classic momo filling in Kathmandu.
Chicken meat: कुखुराको मासु, or just चिकेन.
The prized festival meat, especially at Dashain.
दूध चिया 'milk tea', कालो चिया 'black tea'.
तातो पानी 'hot water' (often drunk plain), उमालेको पानी 'boiled water'.
Also spelled मोमो. Steamed, fried (फ्राइ), or in soup (झोल मःम).

vocab.en: to eat; to drink (tea, water); to smoke
vocab.note: Nepali 'eats' tea and water: चिया खानु. म खान्छु, तपाईं खानुहुन्छ.
Used for alcohol and in more careful speech: पानी पिउनु.
Experiencer verb: मलाई चिया चाहियो 'I want tea'; चाहिँदैन 'don't need'.

vocab.en: to like (lit. to fall into the heart)
vocab.note: मलाई मःम मन पर्छ 'I like momos'.
दिनुहोस् 'please give' — the standard way to order. Past: दियो.
In a dal bhat restaurant, rice and dal refills (थप) are usually free.
Colloquially also भेज bhej; non-veg = ननभेज/मांसाहारी.

phrases.en: Would you like tea or coffee?
Shall I give you a bit more?

grammar.title: The experiencer construction: मलाई …
grammar.body:
Feelings, needs and likes are not things you *do* in Nepali — they *happen to you*. The person who feels them is marked with **-लाई** ('to'), and the verb agrees with the thing felt, not with you:

**मलाई भोक लाग्यो** — 'to-me hunger struck' = I'm hungry.
**मलाई मःम मन पर्छ** — 'to-me momos fall-in-heart' = I like momos.
**मलाई पानी चाहियो** — 'to-me water was-needed' = I want/need water.

Pronoun + लाई: म → **मलाई** · हामी → **हामीलाई** · तिमी → **तिमीलाई** · तपाईं → **तपाईंलाई** · ऊ → **उसलाई** · उनी → **उनलाई** · उहाँ → **उहाँलाई**.

Tense tip: for something you feel **right now**, Nepali uses the past form: भोक लाग्यो, मन पर्‍यो 'I like it (this one I'm tasting)', चाहियो 'I want (now)'. For general truths, use the present: मन पर्छ 'I (always) like', चाहिन्छ 'is needed (in general)'.

Negatives: मन **पर्दैन** 'don't like', **चाहिँदैन** 'don't need', भोक **लागेको छैन** 'I'm not hungry'.

examples.en: I like this pickle. (tasting it now)
We'd like two bottles of water.

grammar.title: Ordering and offering
grammar.body:
To order, name the item and add **दिनुहोस्** 'please give' (casual: दिनुस्). To offer something to a guest, ask with the polite present: **खानुहुन्छ?** 'will you eat/drink?'. Use **कि** 'or' for choices.

Remember that tea, water, coffee and even cigarettes are all *eaten* (खानु) in everyday Nepali. पिउनु 'drink' is for alcohol or sounds a bit bookish.

At a Nepali home your host will keep offering more (**थप**). To refuse politely, say **पुग्यो** 'it's enough' or **पेट भरियो** 'I'm full' — and cover your plate with your hand.

examples.native: म चिया खान्छु, तर कफी खाँदिनँ।
examples.roman: ma chiyā khānchhu, tara kaphi khāṃdinaṃ.
examples.en: I drink tea, but I don't drink coffee.

dialogue.title: At the momo shop
dialogue.setting: Ram takes Tom to a small momo restaurant (खाजा घर) in Kathmandu. A young waiter comes over.

lines.speaker: Ram
lines.native: एक प्लेट बफ मःम र एक प्लेट भेज मःम।
lines.roman: ek pleṭ baph momo ra ek pleṭ bhej momo.
lines.en: One plate of buff momos and one plate of veg momos.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.en: What shall I bring you to drink?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: मलाई एउटा दूध चिया। चिनी कम है।
lines.roman: malāi euṭā dudh chiyā. chini kam hai.
lines.en: A milk tea for me. Not much sugar, OK?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: एकदमै मन पर्‍यो! तर अलि पिरो छ।
lines.roman: ekdamai man paryo! tara ali piro chha.
lines.en: I love them! But they're a bit spicy.

culture: **Dal bhat** is eaten twice a day, late morning and evening — trekkers joke 'दाल भात पावर, २४ आवर' ('dal bhat power, 24 hour'). Most Nepalis eat with the **right hand** only. Be aware of **जुठो** *juṭho*: food or a cup that has touched someone's lips is ritually 'polluted', so don't offer anyone a bite of your food, don't put your fork back into a shared dish, and drink from a shared water bottle by pouring without touching your lips. Tea is milky and sweet; in Newar homes you may be offered **समय बजी** and in the hills **रक्सी** (home-distilled spirit) — it's fine to refuse with पर्दैन, धन्यवाद.

tip.title: Hunger 'happens to' you: मलाई …
tip.body:
- Feelings and needs happen *to* you: the person takes **-लाई**. **मलाई** भोक लाग्यो = 'to me hunger struck' = I'm hungry.
- मलाई, हामीलाई, तिमीलाई, तपाईंलाई, उहाँलाई.
- **मलाई … चाहियो** = I'd like / I need. 'Not': **चाहिँदैन**; भोक **लागेको छैन** 'not hungry'.
tip.pattern: मलाई + भोक / तिर्खा + लाग्यो  ·  मलाई + thing + चाहियो

sentences.en: I don't want any food, thanks.

tip.title: Ordering: … दिनुहोस्
tip.body:
- To order, name the thing and add **दिनुहोस्** 'please give': दुईवटा चिया दिनुहोस्.
- To offer, ask **खानुहुन्छ?** 'will you have?'. Tea, water and coffee are all *eaten* (खानु); पिउनु 'drink' is more careful.
- **कि** = 'or' in a choice: चिया कि कफी?

sentences.en: A plate of veg momos, please.
Didi, would you like tea or water?

sentences.native: एउटा कफी र एउटा चिया दिनुहोस्।
sentences.roman: euṭā kaphi ra euṭā chiyā dinuhos.
sentences.en: One coffee and one tea, please.

tip.title: More? Enough!
tip.body:
- Hosts keep offering **थप** 'more': भात थप्नुहुन्छ? 'More rice?'
- Ask for more yourself: अलिकति थप दिनुहोस् न.
- To say no, say **पुग्यो** 'that's enough' or **पेट भरियो** 'I'm full', and cover your plate with your hand.

sentences.en: Could I have a bit more rice?
That's enough rice, a little more dal.
Brother, could you bring the bill?

tip.title: Talking about taste
tip.body:
- Taste words go before **छ**: मिठो छ 'it's tasty', पिरो छ 'it's spicy'. **अलि** = 'a bit', **धेरै** = 'very'.
- 'Please don't add…' = **न-** + verb + **-नुहोस्**: पिरो **नहाल्नुहोस्** है.
- **कम** = 'less, not much': चिनी कम.
tip.pattern: thing + (अलि / धेरै) + taste + छ  ·  न + हाल्नुहोस्

sentences.en: This pickle is a bit spicy.
Don't put in too much sugar.
No milk in the tea, please.
There's no salt in the curry.
Let's have momos for a snack.

tip.title: 'I like' = मलाई … मन पर्छ
tip.body:
- 'Like' works like hunger: **मलाई** मःम **मन पर्छ** 'to me momos fall in the heart'.
- **मन पर्छ** = you like it in general; **मन पर्‍यो** = you like this one, now.
- 'Don't like' = **मन पर्दैन**. For what you eat, the normal verb: म मासु **खाँदिनँ** 'I don't eat meat'.

sentences.native: म मासु खाँदिनँ, म शाकाहारी हुँ।
sentences.roman: ma māsu khāṃdinaṃ, ma sākāhāri huṃ.
sentences.en: I don't eat meat, I'm vegetarian.
